source: Li et al. (2025) Understanding the Thinking Process of Reasoning Models (Table 2 vs Table 4 text)
finding: The paper states Table 2 (prompting conditions) was run on all annotated data, and Table 4 (classifier comparison) on the 30% test subset only. So the 0.681 vs 0.805 gap for GPT-4.1 Ex+Guide is at least a different evaluation set, not a model change. The paper gives no further explanation.
numbers: Table 2 GPT-4.1 Ex+Guide: paragraph 0.757, sentence 0.681 (all data). Table 4 GPT-4.1 Ex+Guide: 0.805 accuracy, kappa 0.764 (30% test split). Confusion-matrix diagonal on the test split sums to 80.5 (11.3+16.6+5.7+17.1+6.1+18.5+5.2). GPT-4.1 needs no training, so a split effect cannot come from leakage.
quote: These experiments are conducted on all of our annotated data.
limits: The test split is about 30% of 38 responses (roughly 11), so an easy subset is plausible but untested. The paper does not say whether the split was by response or by sentence.
agent_relevance: Treat 0.68 as the safe all-data estimate for a prompt-only labeller with this guidebook; 0.805 is an upper figure on a small subset.

source: Li et al. (2025) Understanding the Thinking Process of Reasoning Models (Section 4.3, Table 4)
finding: Small fine-tuned encoders come close to the best prompt-only labeller on the same 30% test split. Training used 70% of the annotated data.
numbers: BERT 0.732 accuracy / kappa 0.671; RoBERTa 0.730 / 0.670; SVM on Gemini embeddings 0.704 / 0.632; MLP 0.684 / 0.613; KNN 0.587 / 0.490; GPT-4.1 Ex+Guide 0.805 / 0.764.
limits: Fewer than 40 responses, one SAT-math corpus, one model (R1). If the split was by sentence, BERT saw neighbours of test sentences and 0.732 is inflated. No cost or latency figures. Kappa 0.67 is below the 0.75 bar we set for gating.
agent_relevance: A BERT-size labeller is cheap but too weak to gate actions alone; use it for logging only, and a strong labeller offline.

source: Li et al. (2025) ThinkARM (Table 1, gold set annotator agreement)
finding: On the larger ThinkARM gold set (7,067 sentences, eight labels incl. Answer) GPT-4.1 reaches 86.10% accuracy and kappa 82.74 overall, close to GPT-5. This is higher than the 0.805 / 0.681 of the first paper for the same model, so the first paper's gap is more about its small data, guidebook and label set than about the model.
numbers: Overall accuracy / kappa: GPT-4.1 86.10 / 82.74; GPT-5 86.33 / 82.85; Gemini-2.5-Flash 82.90 / 78.67; Gemini-2.5-Pro 80.89 / 75.96. Reasoning-model traces: GPT-4.1 85.75 / 82.39; non-reasoning: 89.34 / 85.36.
limits: Same research group. Gold set built by them; labels differ (eight, with Answer), so this is not a clean replication of Table 2. Kappa is over all labels, not per boundary such as Verify vs Analyze.
agent_relevance: Strong-LLM episode labelling at 85-86% is good enough for offline analysis. Gap 5 is mostly closed: both evaluation set and prompt/label design differ, and neither explains the whole 0.681 to 0.805 gap alone.

source: Zoumpoulidi, Paraskevopoulos, Potamianos (2026) Cognitive Profiling of LRMs' Reasoning Traces Using Bloom's Taxonomy (Section 5.4)
finding: First held-out test found of step-label features against a length-only baseline. L1-regularised logistic regression on 43 features (token count, six Bloom-level token shares, 6x6 transition matrix) beats length alone in AUC, but the gain is modest and accuracy and F1 barely move.
numbers: Nested cross-validation (5 outer, 3 inner folds), 9,132 balanced samples (each model x dataset cell balanced; GSM8K, GSM-hard, MATH500). Full model AUC 0.676 +/- 0.012 vs length-only 0.613 +/- 0.008; accuracy 0.631 vs 0.623; F1 0.667 vs 0.666. Total token count is the strongest negative coefficient (-0.4373). Evaluate-to-Analyze and Analyze-to-Evaluate transitions are negative (-0.1271, -0.1236): oscillation without convergence. Apply-to-Evaluate is the strongest positive.
quote: Applying -> evaluating is the strongest positive coefficient
limits: Bloom labels, not Schoenfeld. Math only, easy-to-medium sets; balanced sampling removes base-rate effects. Folds are probably over samples, not grouped by problem, so difficulty leakage is possible. AUC 0.68 is weak for a gate.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 1 for a close cousin: step-type features add about +0.06 AUC over length. An episode-coded gate would be weak; the oscillation pattern (check, re-analyse, check) is the useful stuck cue.

source: Lee, Queen, Zou (2026) ReasonOps: Operator Segmentation for LLM Reasoning Traces (Section 6.2, Table 3)
finding: Within-problem AUC (WP-AUC) separates correct from incorrect traces on the same problem, which removes difficulty confounds. Length is near chance. Counts of backtrack and wait words do better. Operator features do best. A self-judge by the same model is at chance.
numbers: 44,662 traces, 12 thinking models, 8 benchmarks, problem-level 5-fold CV. WP-AUC: length 0.551 (within-dataset), backtrack count 0.594, wait count 0.603, SelfCheck (model judges own trace) 0.512, Op-XGB 0.701 cross-dataset / 0.723 within-dataset, OST 0.701 / 0.703. Within-dataset Op-XGB: AIME 0.838, LiveCodeBench 0.795. BBH and HumanEval excluded as near chance.
limits: Operators come from unsupervised clustering of sentence-initial 3-token pivots, not Schoenfeld labels. Features include 8,000-dim anchor-phrase TF-IDF. Preprint, one group.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 1 more firmly: with problem difficulty held fixed, length is almost useless and cheap word counts already beat it. A within-problem comparison (ranking N attempts) is the fair test for our agent. Do not ask the same model to judge its own trace.

source: Lee, Queen, Zou (2026) ReasonOps (Section 6.1 easy vs hard; Section 6.3 early prediction)
finding: Reflection helps or hurts depending on difficulty. On easy problems correct traces are committal (forward stepping); on hard problems the signal vanishes and hypothesizing is the only operator that seems to help. Correctness can be predicted from half a trace.
numbers: Easy = more than 2/3 of models solve; hard = fewer than 1/3. Committal-minus-reflective gap on easy problems: +44.2% correct vs +7.5% incorrect, AUC 0.76 [0.74, 0.78]. Hard problems: +30.4% vs +34.9%, Mann-Whitney p=0.15, AUC 0.48 [0.44, 0.51]. Hypothesizing-minus-inferring gap grows to 6.6% at the trace tail on hard problems. Early prediction WP-AUC: 0.605 at 10% of trace, 0.664 at 50%, 0.701 at 100% (AIME: 0.645, 0.740, 0.801).
limits: Difficulty defined by model pass rate, so partly circular. Four benchmarks used for the split.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 8 partly: extra reflection is a symptom on easy items and may be a tool on hard ones. A stuck rule should depend on item difficulty, and half a trace already carries most of the signal.

source: Feng et al. (2025) What Characterizes Effective Reasoning? (Table 1, summary condition)
finding: The editing experiment has a third arm that replaces the failed branch with a short summary. The summary keeps most of the gain for R1 and a variable share for GPT-oss. This answers gap 10 in part: a short note in context works, but not as well as deleting, and it depends on the model.
numbers: Accuracy of 8 continuations per edited CoT, incorrect HARP CoTs, 11,520 continuations in total. R1 first failed branch: original 20.89 +/- 1.36, reduced 29.42 +/- 1.66, reduced with summary 28.14 +/- 1.38. R1 last failed branch: 9.72, 23.75, 22.57. GPT-oss-120B first: 28.05, 36.41, 29.51. GPT-oss last: 16.50, 27.33, 25.22. Share of delete-gain kept by summary (computed): R1 85% and 92%; GPT-oss 17% and 81%.
quote: failed branches harm performance by biasing subsequent exploration
limits: The summary is a concise summary of the failed branch added after the truncated prefix, not a one-line dead-end note. Only continuations from incorrect CoTs, so selection effects. Two models.
agent_relevance: Keep a dead-end note instead of the full text: expect most of the delete gain for R1 but possibly little for GPT-oss on early branches. Test with our own models; make the note say why the branch failed.

source: Feng et al. (2025) What Characterizes Effective Reasoning? (labelling, Review definition, reranking)
finding: Feng's Review label is broader than Schoenfeld Verify: it covers reading, checking, restating, deleting or rewinding existing material without advancing the frontier. The labeller is Llama 4 Maverick at 90% agreement with in-house human labels. So the apparent clash with ThinkARM (Verify helps, Review hurts) compares different categories. Failed-Step Fraction as a selector beats length and review-ratio selectors.
numbers: Review labelled per semantic chunk with 5 chunks of context each side; 90% agreement. 64 candidates per problem, bootstrap with 200 replicates. FSF top-1 selection gains roughly 5-13 on AIME 2025 (text of results truncated in my read; units and per-model values sit in Figure 5). Within the same question, longer CoT and higher review ratio are negatively associated with accuracy, more strongly on harder questions.
limits: Review is not split into early, mid and final. No controlled manipulation of Verify placement. Gain figures read from prose.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open as an experiment but the tension is smaller than thought: Review (re-read plus rewind) is not Verify. Design our test as three arms: no check, final check only, mid-trace checks at a fixed cap.

finding: A prompt-only rule to finish ideas barely helps; TIP helps a little; a selective, scored intervention helps most. The standard prompt was 'Think step by step. Explore each idea thoroughly before moving on.' For gap 6: a pure prompt rule did not reproduce TIP in this test.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, AIME24: vanilla 28.9, standard prompting 29.0, TIP 31.3, SmartSwitch 40.0. The TIP baseline run used a persistence prompt ('Try to complete every idea you think of and don't give up halfway') plus the decoding penalty.
limits: One small model, one benchmark, no seeds or CIs shown. Equal-token comparison not reported. The prompt rule differs from the one we plan.
agent_relevance: A bare prompt rule is not enough on a small distilled model. A scaffold has to act at the switch (check the dropped thought, then deepen or confirm abandon). Not tested on a frontier model with a scaffold.

finding: The perception module spots switch cues ('Alternatively' etc.), cuts the preceding thought, scores it with a process reward model, and only if the score is high injects a 'deepen' prompt (at most three per problem). Intervening at every switch hurts.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on AIME25: no module 20.0; Always Intervene 18.9; Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B 21.1; PRM800K-7B 22.3; PRM-72B 24.8; Universal-PRM-7B 36.7.
limits: Needs a PRM with long context, so not a cheap detector. No precision or recall of the switch-then-abandon flag reported, only end accuracy. Small model.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence on action: a switch-cue counter alone is not a stuck detector. Add a second check on the abandoned thought. Always-on interruption is worse than none.

finding: A one-layer linear probe on the hidden state of the paragraph-break token detects repetitive 'word salad' chunks on the fly. It is the only detector found with measured accuracy against labelled loops. It needs model weights, so it is not for a black-box scaffold.
numbers: Qwen-7B distill, accuracy / AUROC: GSM8K 92.72 / 98.63 (temp 0), MATH-500 92.31 / 95.95, AIME25 89.77 / 95.84, GPQA-Diamond 93.52 / 97.89; at temp 0.6 AIME25 drops to 77.96 / 80.15. Qwen3-8B accuracy 78.0 to 88.1, mean about 83%. More than 55% of tokens in R1-distill GPQA outputs are word salad. Chop after two consecutive detections, then a fixed rescue prompt with a 4k-8k token budget.
limits: Labels are machine-made (chunks after a repetition chopping point), not human stuck points. Accuracy and AUROC, not precision or recall; class balance unclear. White-box only.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 in part: loops are detectable at 78-93% chunk accuracy and the action (cut, short regenerate prompt) works. A text-only version (n-gram repeats) is untested against this probe.

source: ROM: Real-time Overthinking Mitigation via Streaming Detection and Intervention (2026), abstract and Section 3
finding: A small hidden-state detector spots the switch from productive to redundant reasoning around the first correct solution and cuts the trace there. The authors name surface heuristics (entropy, step embeddings, closing-tag attention) as less reliable.
numbers: Probe separates adjacent phases at 85.9% accuracy / AUROC 0.928 (group CV); position-only is chance. Five backbones, five benchmarks, ten baselines: best accuracy in 19 of 25 settings, response length cut 28-77% (mean 45%).
limits: White-box (frozen model, about 0.1% extra parameters). Preprint; baselines run by the authors. Targets overthinking after a correct answer, not stuck states before one.
agent_relevance: Overthinking after a correct answer is detectable inside the model. For a black-box scaffold the equivalent is a cheap answer-stability probe (DEER style). Not tested here.

source: Cuadron et al. (2025) The Danger of Overthinking: Examining the Reasoning-Action Dilemma in Agentic Tasks (Sections 3.3, 5)
finding: Agentic failure labels exist: Analysis Paralysis, Rogue Actions, Premature Disengagement, scored 0-10 by an LLM judge. Agreement with four human experts is shown only as a correlation figure on 20 traces. Picking the lower-overthinking run helps. This is the only agentic evidence for gap 4 and it is about coded overthinking, not Schoenfeld episodes.
numbers: 4,018 SWE-bench Verified trajectories. Lowest-Overthinking@k: k=2 low-effort samples give 27.3% resolved at 43% lower cost than high effort; k=3 gives 30.3% with 15% lower cost. Reasoning models score higher on overthinking than non-reasoning models. Smaller models overthink more.
limits: Judge validated on only 20 traces; no kappa or precision/recall in the text read. No Schoenfeld label mapping. The overthinking score is a ranker across runs, not an online stop.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays mostly open. A cheap use for our agent: when it runs N attempts, rank by a coded stuck score rather than by length.

source: Li et al. (2025) ThinkARM (Table 5 header and rows; Section 2.2)
finding: Re-reading the Table 5 row order shows earlier notes misread the columns. Columns are Read, Analyze, Plan, Implement, Explore, Verify, Answer, Monitor. The values 8.52, 7.31 and 4.63 are the Answer column, not Monitor. L1 Monitor is 1.64%, slightly below the baseline 1.84%. The Answer episode is an extension ThinkARM added for the final commit.
limits: One table, 1.5B models, one corpus. The earlier critique statement that 7.31 and 4.63 were Monitor is also wrong; they are Answer. Verify values 8.37 and 9.94 stand.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 closes by correction: there is no Monitor rise under length penalty. The Answer share rises because answer-writing is a fixed cost (208 vs 376 tokens) over a much shorter trace. Monitor stays near 1.6-1.8% in all four runs.

source: Schoenfeld (1983, 1985, 1987, 1992) and Harskamp and Suhre (2007): access attempt
finding: Tried the author's Berkeley file paths for the 1987 metacognition paper, the 1992 chapter and the 1983 episodes paper (all 404) and the ScienceDirect page for Harskamp and Suhre (403). Nothing could be read. The human baseline numbers (share of attempts with no monitoring, timeline-graph counts) remain unverified.
numbers: No numbers obtained. 2509.14662 describes the theory as built on hundreds of hours of videotaped think-aloud sessions and cites the idea that many students read, pick a path and never reassess; it gives no figure.
limits: Web search quota was exhausted, and arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors during this pass, so no open copies were found.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. Do not put a Schoenfeld percentage in the schema until the 1985 book or the 1992 chapter is read.

source: Li et al. (2025) ThinkARM (guidebook in appendix: Answer and Verify definitions)
finding: The Verify label is defined by checking phrases ('Let me double-check', 'Is there any mistake?', 'Let's try another way to verify'). Answer is a declarative final or provisional answer. Because Answer is separate, Answer-to-Verify means checking right after stating an answer (the final-check pattern). Mid-trace loops are not split out and position was not a feature.
numbers: Eight episodes. The guidebook lists Verify indicator phrases and distinguishing features against Implement and Answer. Provisional answers are also labelled Answer.
limits: Definitions only. No label separates a check before any answer from a check after an answer.
agent_relevance: To test gap 3 our agent needs position-tagged Verify logs (before first answer, after first answer, after a switch).
